title: The inevitable
hook: the reality, what is the reality (69:1–3)

segments.voice: Yesterday: the garden owners, and your line, the poor's share first. Did something get shared from the top? Today a new surah, and it opens with one word, said three times. Day six hundred forty-three.

Most of what fills a day isn't certain. The traffic might clear. The text might get a reply. The stock might go up. The weather app says forty percent. We spend hours on maybes. Now think of the short list of things that are not maybes. The sun will set tonight. You were born. You will die. Surah sixty-nine is named for the thing on that list that people most like to forget. It opens by saying its name, and then asking what it is, twice.
screen: `A SURAH NAMED FOR ONE OF THEM.`

segments.voice: Surah al-Haqqah begins, in Pickthall's translation: "The Reality! What is the Reality?" Then the third verse asks again: and what will make you know what the Reality is? Al-haqqah comes from the root h-q-q, the root of haqq: truth, what is real, what is due, what must come to pass. Translators reach for different words, the Reality, the Inevitable, the Sure Truth, because the Arabic holds all of them. And one of the names of Allah, al-Haqq, the Truth, the Real, comes from the same root. The opening is a teaching device the Qur'an uses more than once: name a thing, then ask what it is, then ask how you could possibly know. It's like someone saying, the thing, what is the thing, you have no idea what the thing is. By the third line, you're leaning in. And what is it? Commentators agree the surah means the Day of Resurrection, the day that is certain to come. But notice the surah doesn't open with a description. It goes straight into history. The peoples of 'Ad and Thamud, who called the coming day a lie, and what happened to them. Pharaoh. The flood in Nuh's time. Before telling you about the day, the surah reminds you that people have been sure it wasn't coming for a very long time. The point isn't fear for its own sake. It's sorting. Some things in your life are maybes. A few are haqq, real and due. The surah asks you to know the difference and live on the real ones.

The practice: think of what is certain. Sit, and let today's maybes come up: the worries, the plans, the waiting. Don't fight them. Set each one to the side, as if on a shelf. Then ask: what's certain? That I'm breathing now. That this day will end. That my life will end too, one day. That I'll be asked what I did with it, Muslims would add. Stay with the short list. Notice how quiet it is. The bell holds the time.
The inevitable. Al-Haqqah, the Reality: the day that is certain to come, from the root of haqq, what is true and due. Today's word.

Your line: what is real. Today, when a maybe starts eating your attention, ask yourself whether it's real and due, or only possible, and give it the attention that matches. Day six hundred forty-three.

howItsDone: Muslims believe in the Last Day as one of the articles of faith; surahs like al-Haqqah, recited in prayer, are a regular reminder of it, and al-Haqq, the Truth, is one of the names of Allah.
